grammar.title: Asking amounts with 幾 + measure word
grammar.pattern: 幾 + measure word (+ noun)？ → answer: 一/二/三/四 + measure word
grammar.explanation: 幾 (jǐ) asks 'how many' when the speaker expects a small number, and it must be followed by a measure word: 幾杯 (how many cups), 幾點 (what time), 幾台 (how many machines/vehicles). You answer by putting the number in exactly the same slot where 幾 was: 幾杯 → 三杯, 幾點 → 四點. The word order of the rest of the sentence never changes.
grammar.contrast: 多少 also means 'how much/how many', but it is used for open-ended or large amounts and normally takes no measure word — prices especially: 多少錢 (how much money). Rule of thumb: if you expect an answer under about ten and there is a measure word, use 幾; if it is money or an unknown big amount, use 多少.
grammar.common_error: Two things. First, learners drop the measure word and say 'jǐ bēi' as just 'jǐ' — 幾 can almost never stand alone in front of a noun. Second, when the number is 2, learners say 'èr bēi'. Before a measure word Taiwanese Mandarin uses 'liǎng' instead; 二 is used for numbers you read out, like table numbers, dates, and phone digits (二號).

passage.title: 早餐店的早上
passage.hanzi: 早上三點半，早餐店的老闆就開了店。外面天沒亮，路上很安靜。四點，一個客人來了，他要一杯熱茶，糖少一點。四點半，人多了起來，老闆忙得沒時間坐下。他說：「開店三年了，我早上四點就起來，不用時鐘。」
passage.gloss: At three thirty in the morning the breakfast shop owner opens up. Outside it isn't light yet and the street is very quiet. At four o'clock a customer comes in; he wants a hot tea with just a little sugar. By four thirty more and more people arrive, and the owner is too busy to sit down. He says, "I've had this shop for three years — I get up at four every morning without needing an alarm clock."

grammar.title: Telling the time: Number + 點, asking with 幾點
grammar.pattern: (Subject +) 幾點 + Verb? → (Subject +) Number + 點 (+ 半) + Verb
grammar.explanation: To say a clock time, put the number straight in front of 點: 五點 (5:00), 六點半 (6:30), 十點 (10:00). The time word goes BEFORE the verb, not after it, so you say 我七點吃飯 (I eat at seven). To ask what time, replace the number with 幾: 你幾點下班? The answer keeps the same word order, just swapping 幾 for a number.
grammar.contrast: 點 vs 號: 五點 is a clock time (5 o'clock), 五號 is a calendar date (the 5th). If someone asks 幾點? answer with a time; if they ask 幾號? answer with a date. Same numbers, totally different question.
grammar.common_error: Learners copy English word order and say 你下班幾點? — putting the time after the verb. In Chinese the time always comes before the verb: 你幾點下班? Another frequent slip is using 多少 to ask the time (✗多少點?); clock times use 幾, never 多少.

passage.title: 我的一天
passage.hanzi: 我早上七點吃早餐,八點騎腳踏車上班。中午和同事吃便當,一個八十塊,很便宜。下午五點下班,我搭捷運,六點半就在家了。晚上九點,我和朋友點一杯咖啡,十點半看書,很舒服。
passage.gloss: I eat breakfast at seven in the morning and ride my bike to work at eight. At noon I have a lunchbox with my colleagues; one costs eighty dollars, which is very cheap. I get off work at five in the afternoon, take the MRT, and I'm home by six thirty. At nine in the evening I order a cup of coffee with a friend, and at ten thirty I read — it's very relaxing.

grammar.title: Counting things: Number + 個/本/些 + Noun, and asking 多少錢
grammar.pattern: Number + 個 / 本 / 些 + Noun　／　(這/那 + 個/本/些 +) Noun + 多少錢？
grammar.explanation: In Chinese a number can never sit straight in front of a noun; a measure word goes in between. 個 is the general one (一個便當), 本 is for books (一本書), and 些 means 'some / a few' and only ever appears as 一些 or 這些/那些 — never with other numbers. To ask a price, put 多少錢 at the end of the sentence: 這本書多少錢？ The answer uses 塊 for dollars: 五十塊。
grammar.contrast: 個 vs 些: use 個/本 when you say an exact number (三個蘋果), use 些 when the amount is vague (一些蘋果). If you can count it out loud, don't use 些.
grammar.common_error: Learners drop the measure word and say 我買一書 or 三便當, and they also try to say 三些蘋果. 些 can only follow 一, 這 or 那 — say 三個蘋果 instead.

passage.title: 逛商店
passage.hanzi: 週末早上，我和朋友一起逛學校附近的商店。商店不大，東西很多，也很便宜。我買了一本書，五十塊；朋友買了一些蘋果和一個便當，一共九十塊。我們用悠遊卡付錢，老闆說謝謝，也說下週再見。天氣很好，我們就騎腳踏車逛了一下，都很高興。
passage.gloss: On the weekend morning, my friend and I browsed the shop near our school. The shop isn't big, but there's a lot of stuff and it's cheap. I bought a book for fifty dollars; my friend bought some apples and a lunchbox, ninety dollars in all. We paid with an EasyCard, and the shop owner said thank you and see you next week. The weather was nice, so we rode our bikes around for a while. We were both very happy.
